newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Investors cautious on Brazil new Banerj sale rules.
newsitem.headline: Investors cautious on Brazil new Banerj sale rules.

text.p: After failing twice last year to sell off its bank, the Brazilian state of Rio de Janeiro is hoping to succeed in privatizing the financial institution next month by offering new inducements, including a lowered base price.
But potential investors said they must first see tender term details and accompanying privatization guidelines before assessing whether to re-submit bid for the state bank, known as Banerj.
Banerj's minimum price was cut to 300 million reais from 480 million reais under the bank's fresh privatization plan announced Monday by Rio de Janeiro state.

The state, which now hopes to privatize the bank on June 20, also allowed investors to pay for 100 percent of Banerj's auction price with privatization bonds, which makes the bank even cheaper as those bonds can be purchased at 60-70 percent of their face value.
Banco Itau, one of the two bidders which had signed up for Banerj's auction in 1996, said it continues to be interested in the bank but is still looking into the new privatization rules.
"The bank is still interested and is likely to participate," said Aldous Galletti, Institutional Relations director at Banco Itau. "But at the moment we cannot make any further comments," he added.
Bradesco, the other bidder, said any analysis of Banerj's new selloff plan for the moment would be premature.
"The bank is waiting for the publication of the new tender documents," a Bradesco spokeswoman said.
New tender details will be published on June 2.
According to Banerj's new privatization rules, new bidders can prequalify for the sale as of Wednesday, while already prequalified investors do not have to prequalify again.
Seven financial institutions had been prequalified for the sales last year, but only Banco Itau and Bradesco went as far as signing up for the auction and were ready to bid.
Rio de Janeiro state also said it will assume all Banerj's debts to its pension fund, which will be covered with a 2.9 billion reais loan by federal mortgage bank Caixa Economica Federal (CEF).
The loan, however, must be approved by the Senate and Rio de Janeiro Legislative Assembly.
The pension-related debt had been a major stumbling block for the bank's privatization.

Rio Planning Secretary Marco Aurelio Alencar told reporters Monday the state has cut Banerj's base price because a number of non-operational assets, including the building where Banerj is headquartered, was taken out of the bank and will not be offered to investors.

The decision was also seen as a way to avoid legal battles. The second attempt to privatize the bank last year was thwarted by a court injunction granted to trade unions alleging that the building was undervalued.
The new minimum price was also based on a capital restructuring. Banerj, formally known as Banco Banerj S/A, has bought control of insurance firm Banerj Seguros.
Under the previous selloff rules, Banerj and Banerj Seguros would be sold together for 480 million reais. Now the bank, including the insurer, will be auctioned off for 300 million reais.

Banerj was split into two units early last year to allow for the bank's privatization -- one, the so-called Banco Banerj S/A, comprising its regular banking operations, and another, Banco do Estado do Rio de Janeiro, to include its unretrievable assets, which is now being liquidated.
Banerj has been under Central Bank control since December 1994 but has been managed by private Banco Bozano Simonsen on behalf of the Central Bank since January 1996.

Alencar refused to predict whether Banerj's new sale plan will draw more investors. But he said foreign banks may be interested in buying Banerj to enter the Brazilian retail market after HSBC Holdings Plc's takeover of retail bank Banco Bamerindus.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485412))
